abstract: Bena, Bian and Giannetti (UBC Sauder and Stockholm School of Economics; NBER conference draft dated July 8, 2026) study how generative AI changed US entrepreneurial entry. Using difference-in-differences designs that compare industries above and below the median in task-level GenAI exposure, measured from Anthropic Economic Index query shares, before and after GenAI's public release (from August 2022), they find that high-exposure industries saw 20% more startup formation than less-exposed industries. The effect is significant from Q1 2023 and grows over time. The entry wave is geographically dispersed beyond venture-capital hubs, and a growing share of the new startups are AI-native rather than merely AI-enabled. Individual entrants are smaller, but aggregate entry raises employment in new firms by 7% and average earnings by 5% in high-exposure industries. Founders increasingly come from high-exposure occupations and emphasize technical, AI-related skills over capital-raising skills.
keyFindings: New firms increased by over 20% more in industries with above-median GenAI exposure after GenAI's introduction (Data Axle establishments founded 2020–2024; Table 3 coefficient 0.212 log points, SE 0.089).
Monthly business applications rose 3.8% more, and corporate business applications 5.5% more, in above-median-exposure sectors (Census BFS, January 2020 to April 2025).
Above-median-exposure industries had a 10% higher probability of any new firm entering in a year after GenAI's diffusion.
Higher entry more than offset smaller firm size, producing a 7% increase in employment and a 5% increase in average earnings in new firms in high-exposure industries.
The authors estimate a 25% drop in the number of employees in GenAI-exposed startups entering after GenAI diffusion.
Among AI-enabled entrants, the share of high-exposure employees at founding rose from 15.6% to 19.8%.
methodology: Industry-level difference-in-differences. Exposure comes from the March 2025 Anthropic Economic Index (task query shares, aggregated to occupation and then industry via O*NET and employment weights), split at the median. Outcomes: Census Business Formation Statistics at the 2-digit NAICS sector-month level (January 2020 to April 2025; about 20 sectors; bootstrap standard errors), Data Axle/InfoGroup single-location firm entry at the 4-digit NAICS industry-year level (2020–2024; 1,430 observations), Census QWI, and Crunchbase startups founded in the US 2020–2024 linked to LinkedIn employee and founder data via Revelio Labs. LLM-assisted pipelines classify startups as AI-enabled or AI-native.
qualifiers: Tier 1 by the repo's convention for NBER-hosted papers, but this is an unrefereed conference draft, not a numbered NBER working paper. Exposure is time-invariant and measured from Claude.ai usage in December 2024, after the treatment began. The BFS analysis has only about 20 sector clusters. The 20% headline has a wide 95% interval (about 4% to 39%). Estimates compare high- and low-exposure industries, so they identify relative, not aggregate, entry effects. Founder matching covers about one-third of Crunchbase startups.
